questions.question: Q1. Starting from the Flory-Rehner equation, what physical trade-off explains why Q increases as the solvent becomes more water-loving (lower χ)?

answers.a: Lower χ reduces elastic energy storage in the crosslinks, allowing the network to expand.
answers.b: Mixing entropy favours bringing water in; lower χ reduces the penalty for mixing, shifting equilibrium toward higher Q.
answers.c: Lower χ increases the crosslink density, which mechanically stretches the chains.
answers.d: Water solubility increases with lower χ, but the gel itself contracts.

explanations.a: Incorrect — The elastic term v_p^(1/3) − v_p/2 does not vanish; it opposes swelling.
explanations.b: Correct — The Flory-Rehner equation balances mixing (ln(1 − v_p) + χv_p²) against elastic restoring force; lower χ shifts the equilibrium toward lower v_p and thus higher Q = 1/v_p.
explanations.c: Incorrect — χ is independent of crosslink density V₁/V_e.
explanations.d: Incorrect — The gel swells, not contracts, when χ is lower.

questions.question: Q2. In the pH-triggered capsule, explain why the opening pH (p50) can be tuned by changing the pKa of the polyacid shell.

answers.a: The Henderson-Hasselbalch ionisation curve shifts; a higher pKa means the shell ionises at higher pH, so p50 moves deeper into the intestine.
answers.b: Higher pKa materials have more permanent charges that do not respond to pH.
answers.c: The pKa directly sets the Donnan osmotic pressure amplitude regardless of pH.
answers.d: Changing pKa alters the polymer chemical structure but not the pH sensitivity.

explanations.a: Correct — α = 1 / (1 + 10^(pKa − pH)); PMAA (pKa 4.3) opens early in the stomach, while custom pKa 6.0 holds until deeper intestinal pH. Tuning pKa shifts when α climbs above ~50%, thus shifting p50.
explanations.b: Incorrect — Weak polyacids always have pH-dependent ionisation.
explanations.c: Incorrect — pKa determines the pH at which α = 0.5, not a constant pressure.
explanations.d: Incorrect — pKa is an intrinsic chemical property that directly sets pH-ionisation coupling.

questions.question: Q3. Derive the actuation stroke ε for a body-temperature valve crossing the LCST, given Q_sw and Q_col.

explanations.a: Incorrect — This is the volume-change ratio, not the linear strain.
explanations.b: Incorrect — This is a volume-normalised difference, not a linear strain.
explanations.c: Correct — The linear actuation stroke scales as the cube root of the volume change: ε = 1 − (Q_col / Q_sw)^(1/3). A gel collapsing from Q_sw = 10 to Q_col = 1.3 gives ε ≈ 1 − 0.24 ≈ 0.76 or 76% linear contraction.
explanations.d: Incorrect — The relationship is not additive in the cube-root terms.

questions.question: Q4. Why does PNIPAM collapse (lose water) above the LCST (~32°C) when most polymers swell on heating?

answers.a: PNIPAM has a very high glass transition temperature.
answers.b: At high temperature, PNIPAM–water hydrogen bonds break, making the polymer–polymer interactions energetically favourable, so water is expelled.
answers.c: The LCST is caused by melting of crystalline regions in the polymer backbone.
answers.d: PNIPAM undergoes a chemical reaction (decomposition) above 32°C.

explanations.a: Incorrect — T_g and LCST are distinct phenomena.
explanations.b: Correct — PNIPAM forms hydrogen bonds with water at low T; at the LCST, thermal energy breaks these bonds and polymer-polymer interactions become enthalpically favourable, causing water to be expelled and the gel to collapse.
explanations.c: Incorrect — PNIPAM's LCST is not a crystallisation phenomenon.
explanations.d: Incorrect — The LCST is a reversible phase transition, not chemical degradation.

questions.question: Q5. In Sub-Calc C, the full width at half maximum (FWHM) of dQ/dT around 32°C determines:

answers.a: How fast the valve returns to its cold state.
answers.b: Whether the gel is PNIPAM or a different material.
answers.c: The maximum swelling capacity of the gel.
answers.d: The sharpness of the temperature switch; a narrower FWHM means a more abrupt actuation over a small ΔT window.

explanations.a: Incorrect — FWHM is not about the time scale of recovery.
explanations.b: Incorrect — Material identity is orthogonal to the FWHM parameter.
explanations.c: Incorrect — Q_sw is set independently by the material composition.
explanations.d: Correct — The sigmoid width w in φ(T) = 1 / (1 + e^((T − 32)/w)) sets how steeply Q changes near 32°C. A small FWHM (narrow w) gives sharp switching; a large FWHM gives gradual change. A sharp switch is desirable for a valve that snaps decisively.

questions.question: Q6. Comparing Sub-Calc E release mechanisms: what distinguishes Fickian diffusion (n ≈ 0.5) from case-II transport (n = 1)?

answers.a: Fickian is passive molecule-by-molecule diffusion through the swollen network; case-II is driven by a sharp swelling front that steadily invades the implant at constant velocity.
answers.b: Fickian diffusion is faster; case-II is slower.
answers.c: Case-II transport occurs only in biological systems; Fickian only in vitro.
answers.d: They are identical processes with different names for historical reasons.

explanations.a: Correct — Fickian diffusion (n = 0.5) is molecular diffusion through a static swollen matrix; case-II transport (n = 1) is zero-order release driven by a sharp moving swelling front. These produce different power-law exponents on a log-log plot of M_t / M_∞ vs. t.
explanations.b: Incorrect — The speed depends on k and geometry; n alone does not determine rate.
explanations.c: Incorrect — Both can occur in vivo and in vitro; the distinction is mechanistic, not environmental.
explanations.d: Incorrect — They represent fundamentally different release mechanisms.

questions.question: Q7. A pH-triggered capsule with f_ion = 0.20 and β = 30 opens from Q ≈ 3.0 in the stomach (pH 1) to Q ≈ 9.0 at pH 7 (small intestine). At pH 8, it reaches Q ≈ 25 and ruptures. Which design parameter would you adjust to prevent rupture while maintaining release at pH 7?

answers.a: Increase the pKa to shift p50 higher, so the intestinal pH never produces excessive Q.
answers.b: Reduce the dry swelling Q_0 to limit the maximum possible Q.
answers.c: Lower f_ion or β to reduce the Donnan amplification, capping Q below the rupture threshold (~24).
answers.d: Increase the UV crosslinking to stiffen the shell material.

explanations.a: Incorrect — Shifting p50 would delay release entirely, not prevent rupture.
explanations.b: Incorrect — Q_0 is a material property (dry neutral swelling) difficult to adjust without reformulation.
explanations.c: Correct — The swelling amplification Q = Q_0 (1 + β · α · f_ion)^(3/5) grows with either β or f_ion. Lowering one of these reduces the peak Q at high pH. A lower β means less Donnan amplification per unit charge, keeping the capsule intact.
explanations.d: Incorrect — Crosslinking stiffens the shell but does not address the osmotic over-swelling.

questions.question: Q8. Why does the Korsmeyer-Peppas power law fail above 60% drug release?

answers.a: The drug degrades chemically at high concentration.
answers.b: Water osmotically re-enters the implant, reversing the release.
answers.c: The gel collapses and stops releasing drug entirely.
answers.d: Boundary effects and gel deformation dominate; the simple diffusion or swelling-front model no longer applies as the implant geometry changes.

explanations.a: Incorrect — Chemical stability is independent of the diffusion model.
explanations.b: Incorrect — Osmotic re-absorption is not why the model fails.
explanations.c: Incorrect — Collapse does not necessarily stop release.
explanations.d: Correct — The Korsmeyer-Peppas power law assumes a semi-infinite geometry with a sharp moving front or uniform diffusion field. Once >60% is released, boundary effects (implant edges, exhaustion, gel geometry change) violate these assumptions and the model breaks down.

questions.question: Q9. Native cartilage stiffness is approximately 0.1–1 MPa. Using E = 3G and G_swollen = G_dry · Q^(-1/3), which strategy is most effective for designing a gel scaffold that lands in this window?

answers.a: Choose any material; cartilage stiffness is independent of hydrogel composition.
answers.b: Start with a material whose G_dry is much higher than the target, then tune crosslink density to set Q so that Q^(-1/3) softening lands E in the cartilage window.
answers.c: Select a low-crosslink-density gel to achieve large Q, then rely on Q^(-1/3) softening to reach the target E.
answers.d: Use a very high crosslink density to maximise stiffness; cartilage-mimicking gels are always the stiffest hydrogels.

explanations.a: Incorrect — E depends crucially on both G_dry and Q.
explanations.b: Correct — Design proceeds by choosing materials with high enough G_dry, then tuning the UV cure dose (crosslink density) to control Q. A higher Q (more crosslinked) reduces Q^(-1/3) softening, raising E; a lower Q (less crosslinked) increases softening and lowers E. The optimum lands in [0.1, 1] MPa.
explanations.c: Incorrect — A low-crosslink gel swells to large Q, but this over-softens it below cartilage stiffness; the strategy is backwards.
explanations.d: Incorrect — Over-crosslinking can make the gel too stiff; the challenge is balancing stiffness against swelling and achieving the narrow tissue window.

questions.question: Q10. In Sub-Calc A, the gripper folds to θ_fold ≈ 90° · (Q^(1/3) − 1) but is capped at 180°. Below 30° the gripper stays essentially flat and fails to grasp. Given the four materials (Alginate χ=0.40, PEG-DA χ=0.45, PNIPAM χ=0.48, pHEMA χ=0.55), which material(s) would you select for a gripper that must fold to ~100°?

answers.a: PEG-DA or PNIPAM; pHEMA alone would over-fold at ~170°, while Alginate risks rupture from excessive Q.
answers.b: Only Alginate, because it has the lowest χ and thus the highest Q.
answers.c: Any material works equally well if crosslinking is adjusted.
answers.d: Only pHEMA, because the highest χ means the most controlled, moderate fold.

explanations.a: Correct — From theory.md: Alginate (χ=0.40) swells so much that θ_fold ≈ 90° · (Q^(1/3) − 1) likely exceeds 160° and closes fully; pHEMA (χ=0.55) gives moderate Q and thus moderate fold (~170°). PEG-DA (χ=0.45) and PNIPAM (χ=0.48) land in an intermediate regime suitable for a ~100° target fold.
explanations.b: Incorrect — Alginate's very high Q (from low χ) would drive θ_fold well past 100°, over-closing the gripper.
explanations.c: Incorrect — While crosslinking affects Q, the material's χ sets the baseline swelling affinity; you cannot completely decouple them.
explanations.d: Incorrect — pHEMA's high χ would give insufficiently high Q for 100°; experiment shows it folds ~170° (over-closed).
